hints: Think about what UV light does to a Cl-Cl bond in the initiation step, and look for the dot symbol that shows an unpaired electron.
walkthrough:
Spot the clue for radicals**
UV light supplies energy to break bonds by homolytic fission. That means the shared electron pair splits evenly, one electron to each atom, giving two species each with an unpaired electron. In symbols you spot them by the dot, like $\text{H}\bullet$.

Apply to methane plus chlorine**
In the initiation step $\text{Cl}_2$ splits to $2\text{Cl}\bullet$. Then in propagation $\text{Cl}\bullet$ abstracts H from $\text{CH}_4$ to give $\text{HCl}$ plus $\bullet\text{CH}_3$. So from the list the two radical particles that appear are $\text{Cl}\bullet$ and $\bullet\text{CH}_3$.

hints: Recall the meaning of hetero in heterolytic, both bonding electrons go to one atom, so think about which charged species this must create.
walkthrough:
Contrast heterolytic with homolytic**
Heterolytic fission means unequal splitting. Both electrons from the covalent bond go to the same atom. That gives one positive ion and one negative ion, not radicals. No dots remain because all electrons are paired.

Break the C-Cl bond in chloromethane**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$, chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so it takes the bonding pair to become $\text{Cl}^{-}$. Carbon is left short of an electron to become the methyl carbocation, $^{+}\text{CH}_3$ or $\text{CH}_3^{+}$.

hints: Picture the positive Tollens' result, a silver mirror, and ask what must happen to $\text{Ag}^{+}$ and to the $\text{-CHO}$ group at the same time.
walkthrough:
Remember what Tollens' does**
Tollens' reagent contains diamminesilver(I) ions, $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{+}$. An aldehyde, $\text{RCHO}$, gives a silver mirror on warming. That mirror is elemental silver, $\text{Ag}$.

Classify the change**
The aldehyde gains oxygen to become a carboxylate ion, $\text{RCOO}^{-}$. Gain of oxygen is oxidation. At the same time $\text{Ag}^{+}$ gains an electron to form $\text{Ag}$, which is reduction. Either name is accepted for this redox pair, most simply oxidation.
Final answer: Oxidation (aldehyde is oxidised to carboxylate, $\text{Ag}^{+}$ is reduced to $\text{Ag}$)

hints: Focus on what joins to what when a carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ reacts with 2,4-DNPH, and what small molecule is lost to make the orange precipitate.
walkthrough:
Picture the 2,4-DNPH reaction**
An aldehyde or ketone $\text{RR'C=O}$ reacts with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, $\text{H}_2\text{N-NHAr}$, to give a bright orange precipitate, the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, $\text{RR'C=N-NHAr}$.

Why this is condensation**
Two molecules join together with loss of a small molecule, here $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ eliminated from the $\text{C=O}$ oxygen plus two H from the $\text{NH}_2$ group: $$\text{RR'C=O} + \text{H}_2\text{N-NHAr} \rightarrow \text{RR'C=N-NHAr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Joining plus loss of water is the definition of condensation.

hints: Compare the functional groups before and after, a ketone $\text{C=O}$ becomes $\text{CH-OH}$, and think about gain of hydrogen in terms of redox.
walkthrough:
Identify the functional group change**
$\text{NaBH}_4$ supplies hydride, $\text{H}^{-}$. A ketone, $\text{RCOR'}$, is converted to a secondary alcohol, $\text{RCH(OH)R'}$. The $\text{C=O}$ double bond becomes $\text{C-O}$ single plus new $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ bonds.

Classify as redox**
Gain of hydrogen (or hydride) and loss of the C to O bond order is reduction. The overall change can be written: $$\text{RCOR'} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{RCH(OH)R'}$$ So the reaction type is reduction.

hints: Look at the $\text{C=O}$ double bond in the aldehyde and count atoms in the product cyanohydrin to see if anything is lost or only added.
walkthrough:
Write the product**
An aldehyde $\text{RCHO}$ reacts with $\text{HCN}$ to give a hydroxynitrile (cyanohydrin), $\text{RCH(OH)CN}$. Nothing is lost, the H adds to the oxygen and the CN adds to the carbon.

Why this is addition**
The $\text{C=O}$ pi bond breaks and two new sigma bonds form, $\text{C-CN}$ and $\text{O-H}$: $$\text{RCHO} + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{RCH(OH)CN}$$ Two reactants combine to one product with no side product, which is addition, specifically nucleophilic addition.
